Holt A. Sakai 1,2,3,5, Sarah E. Pierce1,2,3,5, Allen Y. Jiang 1,2,3, Ana Cristian1,2,3, Meirui An 1,2,3, Chae Rin Kim2,4, Nouraiz Ahmed1,2,3, Colin F. Hemez1,2,3, Y. Allen Tao1,2,3, Emily Zhang 1,2,3, Sophia J. Wu1,2,3 & David R. Liu 1,2,3

The performance of prime-editing (PE) systems has been improved by systematic engineering of their protein and small RNA components but the structured RNA motifs appended to the 3′ end of PE guide RNAs (pegRNAs)—a key determinant of pegRNA stability and editing efficiency—have not been extensively studied. We introduce PE-PRISM, a high-throughput pooled screen to identify and optimize these 3′ RNA motifs in human cells. Here, using PE-PRISM, we evaluated 2,858 RNA motifs across four iterative libraries, including natural and engineered pseudoknots, G-quadruplexes and reverse transcriptase recruitment elements. We applied structure-guided mutagenesis and combinatorial variant screening to refine hits, culminating in the engineered and evolved pseudoknot variants tevo2.0, eHAV and eSBRMV1-A. In a screen correcting 847 pathogenic ClinVar variants, the top-performing motifs improved PE efficiency over the widely used tevopreQ1 motif for >90% of edits. They also increased PE efficiencies for correcting disease-associated mutations in primary human cells and in vivo in mouse brain and liver.

Prime editing (PE) enables the precise installation of virtually any targeted DNA change, including base substitutions, deletions and small insertions, without requiring double-stranded breaks or exogenous donor DNA1. PE uses a reverse transcriptase (RT) and a programmable nickase such as Cas9 nickase, guided by a PE guide RNA (pegRNA) that specifies both the target locus and the desired edit. Upon Cas9 binding and nicking, the pegRNA’s primer-binding site (PBS) anneals to the nicked DNA strand, priming reverse transcription of an RT template (RTT) and incorporating the desired edit directly into the genome (Fig. 1a)2–4. PE has been applied extensively in basic science5–9, agriculture10–14 and therapeutics15–24. For example, PE precisely corrected a 2-bp deletion in NCF1 in the hematopoietic stem cells of patients with chronic granulomatous disease, resulting in restoration of NADPH oxidase activity in blood cells and clinical benefit25. Virtually all applications of PE would benefit from systems with increased efficiency that could enable new applications, enhance efficacy for clinical use and increase desired signals in basic science studies.

We and others have extensively improved different components of PE systems. These efforts include the use of protein engineering and continuous evolution campaigns to identify Cas9 variants and RT orthologs that support more efficient PE26, genetic screens that have identified cellular determinants of PE outcomes, leading to strategies for enhancing PE efficiency through mismatch repair evasion27–29 or other endogenous factors30, and machine-learning-based tools that guide pegRNA design across many variables including PBS length, RTT length and the strategic coinstallation of silent mutations31–33. We also reported the design of engineered pegRNAs (epegRNAs) that include a structured pseudoknot motif positioned 3′ of the PBS to shield the pegRNA from exonucleolytic degradation34 and others have described similar protective designs35,36. However, while the protein and RNA components of the PE system have systematically been improved through evolution or large-scale screening efforts, the structured motifs within epegRNAs have remained underexplored by comparison, with the vast majority of current PE efforts using the motif we first reported in

We hypothesized that mining a broader diversity of structured 3′ motifs from naturally occurring RNAs could reveal additional elements capable of protecting epegRNA structure and supporting efficient PE without increasing the size of the prime editor protein or epegRNA constructs (Fig. 1b). A systematic evaluation and iterative optimization of structured 3′ RNA motifs could broaden the capabilities of PE in several ways. First, because structured motifs can influence pegRNA secondary structure in an edit-dependent manner34,42, a diverse set of high-performance motifs would facilitate screening designs that minimize adventitious unproductive RNA folding. Second, the identification of smaller, more compact motifs would improve the synthetic accessibility of epegRNAs, particularly for RNA-based or ribonucleoprotein (RNP)-based delivery systems including lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulations, as shorter RNA oligomers are synthesized with higher average yield and purity43.

The most common motif in epegRNAs for current PE workflows is a trimmed and engineered variant of the prequeosine1-1 riboswitch aptamer pseudoknot (tevopreQ1)34,37. Although its inclusion modestly increases pegRNA length by 37 nt, this protective motif can substantially enhance PE efficiencies and is compatible with U6 promoter-driven expression systems such as those in plasmids and adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors. Nevertheless, the limited commercial availability of long synthetic pegRNAs containing tevopreQ1 remains an important factor because of current challenges in chemical synthesis, which becomes more difficult for each additional nucleotide38,39. Alternative semisynthetic approaches have been proposed to bypass these limitations40. In addition, fusion of the prime editor to the N-terminal domain of La, termed PE7, has been shown to stabilize pegRNAs lacking structural motifs by binding the poly(U) tail appended by Pol III during transcription28. Third, the availability of sequence-orthogonal motifs would support twin and multiplexed PE applications by allowing simultaneous use of multiple epegRNAs while reducing the risks of recombination or template switching in viral vectors44–46. Lastly, we reasoned that structured motifs—especially those derived from diverse natural RNAs—could confer additional benefits, such as enhanced transcript expression47, improved Cas9 binding or target site engagement48 and altered subcellular localization49. Motivated by these opportunities, we developed a system for the discovery and optimization of epegRNA structured 3′ motifs from a broad search much larger than the process we used to identify tevopreQ1 (ref. 34). Here, we report the design of a pooled PE reporter system, PE-PRISM (PE pooled reporter for identification of structured motifs), which enables high-throughput discovery of RNA motifs that enhance editing efficiency. Using this system, we performed iterative pooled screens to assess 2,858 total RNA motif candidates derived from diverse natural and synthetic origins and identified several candidates that support robust PE. We demonstrated the broad applicability of these engineered 3′ motifs in the PE-mediated correction of 847 pathogenic mutations in the ClinVar33,50 database. The resulting data reveal three refined motifs that consistently outperform tevopreQ1. We further established the generality of these 3′ motifs across different cell types and delivery modalities, including engineered virus-like particles (eVLPs) and LNP settings in vivo.

Results Design of PE-PRISM We curated a diverse library of structured RNA motif sequences from both natural and synthetic origins. Given the prior benefits of the tevopreQ1 pseudoknot34, we selected pseudoknot sequences51,52 derived from a variety of organisms and functional RNA contexts, including viral 5′ or 3′ UTRs, frameshifting signals and tRNA-like structures (Fig. 1c). In addition to pseudoknots, we included G-quadruplexes, a structurally privileged class of functional RNA motifs53,54, from both natural and synthetic origins55–57. We also selected RNA substructures (hairpins, loops and helices) derived from naturally occurring sequences associated with priming or initiation for the RTs from the Ec48 retron58 (PE6a), M-MLV59 (PEmax and PE6d) and Tf1 retrotransposon60 (PE6c) (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Lastly, we diversified tevopreQ1 to generate variants with all possible single-nucleotide substitutions. In total, we included RNA pseudoknots (n = 189), G-quadruplexes (n = 67), RT recruitment or initiation motifs (n = 39) and variants of tevopreQ1 (n = 143), as well as previously reported sequences as controls (n = 22), in a curated list of 460 structured sequences for assessment in PE. Inspired by recent pooled pegRNA screens9,32,33, we designed a pooled lentiviral library of self-targeting elements, in which each construct contained an epegRNA bearing a unique 3′ motif adjacent to its corresponding target site for PE (Fig. 1d). Although we considered alternative strategies—such as phage-assisted evolution26,61 or enrichment-based selections28,62–64—we prioritized a screening format that could evaluate motif performance across diverse edit types and within the context of human cells given the strong edit dependence of PE outcomes and the likely influence of cellular processes such as RNA expression and degradation34. For the v1 PE-PRISM library, we incorporated the 460 curated RNA motifs into nine previously reported pegRNAs26,27 targeting a representative set of edit types, including transitions, transversions and a small deletion and spanning a range of reported efficiencies (3–55%). We paired each epegRNA–motif combination with its synthetic target site, transduced HEK293T cells with the lentiviral library at low multiplicity of infection (MOI ≤ 0.3) and evaluated PE efficiencies with PEmax, PE6a-g or PE7 (Fig. 1d,e and Methods). We quantified editing outcomes by aligning reads to the full reference amplicon and applying quality and depth thresholds (Extended Data Fig. 1b and Methods). After filtering, the v1 PE-PRISM dataset comprised editing data for 457 motifs

across nine target protospacers and nine prime editor constructs, with two biological replicates per condition (Supplementary Table 2).

PE-PRISM identifies motifs that support efficient editing comparable to tevopreQ1 To compare motifs across different prime editors and target protospacers, we calculated an average z score as a composite metric to account for variability across replicates, editors and target protospacers (Extended Data Fig. 1c–f and Methods). We also accounted for overall library representation of each motif after filtering thresholds were applied (Fig. 1f, left). Negative controls included no motif, random sequence or a variant of tevopreQ1 containing a single-point mutation that disrupts pseudoknot folding (‘dead’)34. Among the top-scoring motifs (Fig. 1f, right), we identified a set of pseudoknot motifs with performance comparable to that of tevopreQ1 (average z = 0.85), including sequences derived from the human signal recognition particle (HSRP; average z = 0.94), wild cucumber mosaic virus (WCMV; average z = 0.86), human parechovirus 1 (HPeV1; average z = 0.75), soil-borne rye mosaic virus (SBRMV1; average z = 0.67) and hepatitis A virus (HAV; average z = 0.60), among many other identified candidates (Fig. 1g). G-quadruplexes and RT initiation motifs did not improve PE outcomes compared to pseudoknots (Extended Data Fig. 1g–i) nor did tevopreQ1 substitution variants (Extended Data Fig. 1j). Together, these data demonstrate that the design and application of our PE-PRISM approach can rapidly nominate 3′ structured motifs that support efficient PE from a broad initial pool of candidate sequences. To cross-validate the nominated motifs from the pooled lentiviral screen, we selected a set of 16 motif pseudoknots for further characterization at six endogenous genomic targets. In HEK293T cells, pooled self-targeting lentivirus and arrayed plasmid transfection editing outcomes were moderately correlated (r = 0.39, 0.64 and 0.53 for PEmax, PE6c and PE7, respectively) and revealed similar trends in PE efficiency (Extended Data Fig. 2a–c). Higher efficiencies with lentiviral delivery may arise from more persistent epegRNA expression, higher local epegRNA concentration proximal to the target site and preferential lentiviral integration at open chromatin65. For treatment with PEmax or PE6c, we found that the pseudoknot hits performed comparably to tevopreQ1 (Extended Data Fig. 2d,e). For PE7, although absolute editing levels remained similar to those of PEmax and PE6c, the structured motifs showed little benefit over the unstructured dead control (Extended Data Fig. 2f), consistent with previous observations28 and our own data (Fig. 1h and Extended Data Fig. 2g), suggesting that steric occlusion disrupts La binding to the 2′ hydroxyl groups of polyuridylated termini, as previously demonstrated28. Collectively, these experiments show that use of naturally occurring pseudoknots as 3′ epegRNA motifs can support efficient PE at endogenous genomic targets by plasmid transfection despite diverse motif evolutionary origins and natural functions.

Targeted mutagenesis of pseudoknots improves PE outcomes We next sought to improve the performance of pseudoknots by introducing targeted mutations to sample local regions of RNA sequence space near these wild-type pseudoknots. On the basis of predicted secondary structure52, we removed unpaired leader and trailing sequences. We introduced targeted single-point mutations (insertions, deletions and substitutions) in unpaired loop regions, as well as paired double mutations in base-paired regions, hypothesizing that preserving pseudoknot structure would yield more active variants (Fig. 2a, left). We applied this structure-guided approach to the top 13 pseudoknots nominated by the v1 screen less than 40 nt in length, generating a collection of 2,044 sequence variants (Fig. 2a, right). As before, we appended these motifs combinatorially to pegR- NAs specifying five diverse prime edits and paired the resulting epegRNAs with their cognate synthetic target sites in a v2 PE-PRISM lentiviral library. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that structure-based mutagenesis yielded engineered pseudoknot variants with improved activities (average z = 0.90) over their naturally occurring precursors (average z = 0.45, 2.0-fold improvement with PEmax, P = 0.0004; Fig. 2c). We performed a reversion analysis of the top-performing motif variant derived from the FMDVA-2 pseudoknot (Fig. 2d). Removal of unpaired trailing nucleotides52 did not reduce activity (average z = 0.18 and 0.32, respectively) relative to the wild-type starting point (average z = 0.07), consistent with our observations across all trimmed library elements (Extended Data Fig. 3f). After trimming, the highest-activity mutations were paired double-nucleotide insertions at position 5, with a slight preference for the U:G wobble base pair (average z = 1.00) over A:U (average z = 0.91) (Fig. 2d). These findings establish that our workflow can readily identify the effects of single-nucleotide and double-nucleotide variants of structured motifs on PE efficiency. To study the global features of the RNA sequence landscape, we categorized changes in the A+U and G+C nucleotide content of sequence variants and quantified the accompanying average performance penalty across the mutants in the library (Fig. 2e). Mutations that resulted in no net change in nucleotide composition impaired wild-type motif performance (average ∆z = −0.14) and most other changes resulted in similarly detrimental or worse outcomes, with notable exceptions for (1) a net single insertion of a G or C (average ∆z = −0.01) and (2) a double substitution of an AU pair with a GC pair (average ∆z = −0.06). That a majority of variants underperform relative to their progenitors—even among structure-based mutations aimed at preserving secondary structures—underscores the complexity of the pseudoknot mutational landscape in the context of PE. Together, these observations highlight the importance of iterated high-throughput parallel screening with PE-PRISM in identifying successful RNA motif sequences for further development.

Combinations of beneficial mutations further enhance pseudoknot performance We next asked whether combining mutations from multiple high-activity variants could further enhance PE efficiency. We selected top-scoring variants for further combinatorial screening and generated pairwise combinations of mutations derived from tevopreQ1 (n = 130), SBRMV1 (n = 92), HPeV1 (n = 84), FMDVA-2 (n = 73) and HAV (n = 38). We also included five motif variants and combinations from other lower-activity lineages (Ec, FMDVO-3, FMDVO-4, PhyMV, TMEV and WCMV) to avoid bottlenecking of sequence diversity. We assembled a v3 PE-PRISM library with 13 different prime edits (comprising 5,889 pegRNAs in total) and measured motif performances with PEmax, PE6c or PE7 (Fig. 2f,g, Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table 4). We observed that combinations of mutations (average z = 0.45) conferred modest improvement over v2 variants (average z = 0.36, paired t-test, one-tailed P = 0.0098; Fig. 2h). Analysis of the top-scoring tevopreQ1 derivative (tevo2.0) revealed an additive benefit (average z = 0.67) of combining a double substitution (hp10 UA > CG, average z = 0.17) and double insertion (hp2 UA, average z = 0.50) (Extended Data Fig. 4b). These observations suggest that beneficial effects of pseudoknot mutations in some cases can be combined to boost PE outcomes beyond improvements from mutations in isolation. We performed arrayed validation for eight v3 motifs selected on the combined basis of (1) aggregate normalized editing efficiencies; (2) consistency of improvement across target protospacers in the v3 library; and (3) diversity of precursor sequences. We tested motif performance both by plasmid transfection (Fig. 2i) and by lentiviral transduction (Fig. 2j), between which we observed moderate correlation (average Pearson r = 0.82 across replicates; Extended Data Fig. 4c–e). For each unique condition (prime editor, target edit and replicate), we ranked motifs by editing efficiency and calculated rank order

distribution. In contrast to the low ranking of tevopreQ1 (rank 1 in 4/63 and 9/72 conditions for plasmid transfection and lentiviral transduction, respectively), the combination mutant tevo2.0 demonstrated the highest performance across both experimental contexts (rank 1 in 18/63 and 20/72 conditions for plasmid transfection and lentiviral transduction, respectively) (Fig. 2i,j). We observed up to 1.2-fold average PE efficiency improvement over tevopreQ1 for top v3 motifs eFMDVA-2.2 and eFMDVO-4 (Extended Data Fig. 4f). In summary, these data indicate that engineered pseudoknot variants bearing combinations of beneficial mutations can further enhance PE activity, demonstrating how the iterative process of diversification and screening using the PE-PRISM system can enable the directed evolution of RNA pseudoknots to identify variants with synergistic combinations of beneficial mutations.

Engineered motifs improve PE efficiencies across cell lines and primary human cell types To systematically explore potential cell line-dependent differences between motif activities, including because of differential expression of RNases or small RNA stabilization factors across cell types (Extended Data Fig. 5a), we tested 12 pegRNA-stabilizing motifs with eight target protospacers, transduced HEK293T, HeLa, K562, U2OS, or N2a cells and assessed editing with PEmax, PE6c or PE7 editors. We observed comparable correlation between different editors for a given cell type (Pearson r = 0.58–0.89) as between the same editor across cell types (Pearson r = 0.63–0.84) (Extended Data Fig. 5b). We observed consistent trends in performance at each of the eight assayed PE target protospacers between cell lines (Fig. 3a). For example, top v3 motif tevo2.0 (average z = 0.72) showed improved activity over tevopreQ1 (average z = 0.12). Our data also revealed that at least one new motif surpassed tevopreQ1 at a majority of edits for each cell context (Extended Data Fig. 5c). We analyzed the frequency distributions of motif rankings, which revealed similar trends in relative performance between cell lines that broadly favored the mutant tevo2.0 over tevopreQ1 among the top three motifs in the majority of conditions (for tevo2.0 versus tevopreQ1: 81% versus 46% in HEK293T, 81% versus 35% in HeLa, 71% versus 33% in U2OS and 100% versus 35% in N2a cells; Fig. 3b). These data demonstrate that improvements to the PE system with engineered pseudoknots translate across a variety of different cell lines. Next, we investigated the compatibility of 3′ structural motifs with additional delivery modalities. We sought contexts in which editing reagents, because of the limited lifetimes of RNA and protein components, would be subjected to much more stringent kinetic requirements for efficient PE, which requires many more bond-forming and bond-breaking events than base editing or nuclease editing. eVLPs66 support efficient and transient delivery of RNP complexes, including prime editors67,68. To test the activity of the set of six leading pseudoknots alongside tevopreQ1 and negative control motifs, we used the v3b PE-eVLP architecture to incorporate these motifs into epegRNAs targeting four highly optimized edits in human HEK293T and mouse N2a cells. Engineered motifs offered substantial improvement in editing over tevopreQ1 at Dnmt1 (33% with tevo2.0 and 12% with tevopreQ1; 2.8-fold improvement), Col12a1 (3.1% with eFMDVO-4 and 2.2% with tevopreQ1; 1.4-fold improvement) and HEK3 (9.4% with tevo2.0 and 6.9% with tevopreQ1; 1.4-fold improvement) and similar efficiencies at FANCF (1.5% with tevo2.0 and 2.0% with tevopreQ1) at the lowest tested dose (approximately 1.3 × 108 eVLPs per μl; Methods), with similar trends observed upon dose escalation (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6a). We also compared these eVLP-delivered PE outcomes with those from low-dose plasmid transfection (1/25th of standard treatment) targeting the same four edits, observing a 1.2-fold improvement in average PE efficiency at Dnmt1 (51% with eHAV and 46% with tevopreQ1), Col12a1 (33% with eFMDVO-4 and 26% with tevopreQ1), HEK3 (14% with eFMDVO-4 and 12% with tevopreQ1) and FANCF (34% with HAV and 29% with tevopreQ1) (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 6b). as well as modality-dependent editor lifetime and durability of expression71 (Fig. 5a). On the basis of the improvement of tevo2.0 over tevopreQ1 that we previously observed for in vitro editing at Dnmt1 in cultured N2a cells with PE-eVLPs, we produced large-scale batches of these v3b PE-eVLPs for in vivo experiments67 and validated batch performance in vitro in N2a cells (Extended Data Fig. 8a,b). When C57BL/6J mice were treated with eVLPs delivered by P0 intracerebroventricular (ICV) administration (5 × 1010 eVLPs per mouse), tevo2.0 yielded a 2.6-fold improvement in Dnmt1 + 2 GTCG > CAAC PE efficiency over tevopreQ1 (0.89% with tevopreQ1 and 2.28% with tevo2.0 in bulk cortex) (Fig. 5b). These observations suggest that, under stringent kinetic regimes in vivo, in which epegRNA lifetime and activity are bottlenecks for PE efficiency, the engineered and evolved 3′ motifs substantially improve outcomes for systems that express epegRNAs only transiently. To assess the potential benefit of our compact, structured motifs on PE with LNPs (PE-LNPs), we used a recently developed in-house LNP formulation relying on an OF-02 ionizable cationic lipid72 to deliver an admixture of PE reagents at an optimized ratio (Methods) targeting mouse Pcsk9 and Dnmt1 loci in Hepa1-6 cells (Extended Data Fig. 8d) and in adult mouse liver (single retro-orbital (RO) injection, 1.7 mg kg−1; Fig. 5c). Discussion The expression level and lifetime of pegRNAs are critical determinants of PE efficiencies, especially under RNA-limiting conditions such as transient delivery in vivo67,79. Given the key role of cellular RNA turnover processes28,34, we sought to assess and iteratively optimize the functional performance of many pegRNA structural motifs by developing the PE-PRISM system. Through iterative mutagenesis and screening, we evaluated 2,858 structured RNA motifs to identify a set of highly active pseudoknot variants that consistently outperformed previous state-of-the-art tevopreQ1 in correcting 847 pathogenic alleles, improving PE across cell types and delivery modalities in cultured cells and in vivo. In practice, our data demonstrate that testing three of our top-performing variants—eHAV, tevo2.0 and HAV—is sufficient to identify a pseudoknot motif that outperforms tevopreQ1 in the vast majority of cases. If the PE application requires the most efficient editing outcomes possible, we recommend testing six motif variants (eHAV, tevo2.0, HAV, eSBRMV1-A, FMDVA-2 and tevopreQ1; motif sequences in Supplementary Table 8) to sample distinct regions of RNA sequence space, prioritized by likelihood of improvement (Fig. 4d). For synthetic epegRNAs, the relatively short eSBRMV1-A (27 nt) consistently performed well (Figs. 3e,f and 5c), suggesting the importance of balancing length-based and activity-based factors in synthetic epegRNA selection. In translational contexts, the set of top-performing motifs identified in this study is especially relevant given that the remainder of pegRNA components (spacer, RTT and PBS) may not be readily changed to avoid unproductive RNA conformations or secondary structures42 (Supplementary Discussion). Given that no motif was universally superior in large-scale screens, we recommend optimization of motif selection as the final stage of the epegRNA development process for practical applications of PE. The target sequence dependence of motif performance, as observed directly in the v4 PE-PRISM screen, cautions against ‘overfitting’ optimal solutions with reporter-based selections that rely on a single (or even a few) edits for identifying improved editor systems. Indeed, while we observed strong final performance of the wild-type HAV motif in the v4 screen (847 edits), earlier screens with fewer edits (up to 13) identified seemingly better alternatives that did not prove superior in broader contexts. We also observed, most clearly in the v4 screen, that the engineered motifs may also improve PE7 activity compared to unstructured or absent motifs (Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 7c,d), suggesting that experiments with a modest number of target sites may underestimate potential effect sizes. These observations highlight the importance of testing enhancements across the widest possible range of prime edits and underscore the advantages of the high-throughput PE-PRISM approach for parallelizing evaluation. The recommended set of RNA motifs improve average editing outcomes without increasing the length of epegRNAs compared to tevopreQ1 and, therefore, should not complicate chemical synthesis or compromise compatibility with size-limited dual-AAV architectures. PE7 constructs, which add an additional 600 bp, typically did not substantially increase PE efficiencies when using the evolved structured pseudoknot motifs across multiple independent experiments (Extended Data Figs. 2f,g and 4c,d). We speculate that structured RNAs sterically antagonize La binding, in agreement with prior studies28. Regardless, pseudoknot-mediated or La-mediated stabilization seem to offer complementary strategies for enhancing PE and their adoption

will likely be use case specific. The continued growth of therapeutic PE, particularly using transient delivery modalities that intentionally minimize exposure to editing reagents, underscores the potential practical impact of this work to enhance state-of-the-art PE outcomes in pegRNA-limited contexts. While motif performance remains edit and context dependent, future advancements resulting in more substantial improvements may reduce this dependency as editing efficiencies approach saturation. Further investigation of the interplay between epegRNA structure and functional performance may reveal the mechanistic basis of sequence-specific enhancements. While we tested over 2,500 distinct RNA motif sequences in this study, our final candidates bear only four or fewer mutations from starting sequences, suggesting that additional rounds of PE-PRISM mutagenesis and screening may yield further benefit. Lastly, PE-PRISM may be broadly useful for identifying modulatory sequence motifs that fine-tune orthogonal biological mechanisms beyond exonuclease stabilization. For example, future implementations could explore sequence motifs designed to bias subcellular localization, enhance facilitated recycling of transcriptional machinery or promote RT recruitment. Alternative screening conditions, such as more limiting or transient expression of epegRNAs, may further increase screening stringency and identify motif sequences that alleviate other bottlenecks associated with different efficiency-limiting regimes. Beyond PE, the PRISM screening system could in principle be applied to other small RNA-based therapeutics, such as sgRNAs for base editing or therapeutic tRNAs, for which sequence motifs may enhance cellular outcomes.

Methods General molecular biology and cloning Primers were ordered from Integrated DNA Technologies. All plasmids, including self-targeting lentiviral elements, PE-PRISM libraries, epegRNA expression plasmids and eVLP plasmids, were cloned by isothermal assembly using NEBuilder HiFi DNA assembly master mix (New England BioLabs, E2621) with DNA inserts from Integrated DNA Technologies (eBlocks or gBlocks) or Twist Bioscience (gene fragments without adaptors) and backbones amplified by PCR with Q5 Hot Start high-fidelity 2× master mix (New England BioLabs, M0494), unless otherwise indicated. For arrayed lentiviral transfer plasmids for self-targeting lentiviral elements, assemblies using PCR-amplified backbone from pSEP308 plasmid80 were transformed into NEB 5-alpha competent cells (New England BioLabs, C2987). For epegRNA plasmids for transfection, assemblies using PCR-amplified backbone from pU6-pegRNA-GG-acceptor plasmid (Addgene, 132777) were transformed into One Shot Mach1 cells (Invitrogen, C862003). Plasmids were purified by Qiagen Plasmid Plus 96 miniprep kits (16181), Qiagen Plasmid Plus midi kits (12943) or Qiagen Plasmid Plus maxi kits (12963). Cloning backbones and primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1.

General mammalian cell culture conditions HEK293T (ATCC, CRL-3216), N2a (CCL-131), HeLa (CCL-2), K562 (CCL- 243) and U2OS (HTB-96) cell lines were purchased from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC). Gesicle 293T cells were purchased from Takara (632617). HEK293T, Gesicle 293T, HeLa and N2a cells were cultured in DMEM with GlutaMAX (Gibco, 10569044) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS (Gibco, 16000044). K562 and U2OS cells were cultured in RPMI 1640 medium with GlutaMAX (Gibco, 61870127) and McCoy’s 5A (modified) medium (Gibco, 16600082), respectively, supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS (Gibco, 16000044). G-CSF-mobilized human CD34+ HSPCs from unidentified healthy adult donors (Fred Hutchinson Research Center) were cultured in X-VIVO-10 (Lonza, 04-380Q) medium supplemented with 100 ng µl−1 human stem cell factor (Peprotech, 300-07), 100 ng µL−1 human thrombopoietin (Peprotech, 300-18) and 100 ng µl−1 human FLT3 ligand (Peprotech, 300-19) at a density of 1 × 106–2 × 106 cells per ml, as previously described16. Primary mouse fibroblasts were isolated from tail dissections and cultured in DMEM with GlutaMAX (Gibco, 10569044) supplemented with 20% (v/v) FBS (Gibco, 16000044) and 1× penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15070063), as previously described15. Immortalized bronchial epithelial 16HBEge-F508del cells (16HBE14o- cells homozygous for F508del and M470; gifts from the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation Therapeutics Lab) were cultured in minimum essential medium (Gibco, 11095-072) supplemented with 10% (v/v) FBS (Gibco, 16000044) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (Gibco, 15070063). Tissue culture dishes were pretreated at 37 °C 5% CO2 for 2 h with LHC-8 basal medium (Gibco, 12678017) supplemented with 1.34 µl mL−1 of 7.5% (v/v) BSA (Gibco, 15260037), 10 µl ml−1 bovine collagen solution type 1 (Advanced Bio- Matrix, 5005-100 ML) and 10 µl ml−1 fibronectin from human plasma (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 33016015), as previously described17. All cell lines tested negative for Mycoplasma and were authenticated by their suppliers. All cell lines were cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO2.

Design of v1 screen Pseudoknot sequences were extracted from PseudoBase52. G-quadruplexes were selected from previously reported sequences or designed according to the pattern (G3N1)4, (G3N2)4 or (G3N3)4, in which three-guanine tracts are separated by randomized loop sequences of 1–3 nt55–57. RT-specific motifs were manually designed from subsets of secondary structures (stem-loop and hairpin motifs) from the murine proline tRNA59, the msDNA RNA–DNA hybrid of the Ec48 retron and the self-priming region of the Tf1 mRNA60. Lastly, all possible single-nucleotide variants of tevopreQ1 were designed and included in

the v1 library. Next, motifs were filtered to (1) exclude sequences with G+C content exceeding the range 20–80%, (2) enforce a maximum pseudoknot length of 50 nt; and (3) remove elements with oligo-U tracts ≥ 4 nt that would terminate RNA polymerase III transcription. Including five random controls, final selected motif designs (n = 460) were paired combinatorially with pegRNAs specifying nine previously developed prime edits26,27 and one nontargeting control pegRNA (targeting mouse Dnmt1) to arrive a list of 4,600 epegRNAs. These assembled epegRNAs were paired with an adjacent synthetic target site (43–44 nt in length); the negative control was paired with a scrambled target site. Each epegRNA–target site element was assigned a unique 10-nt barcode, which was split into 5-nt halves that flanked the synthetic target site immediately following the U6 terminator. The length of library elements was standardized using randomized variable-length linkers with balanced G+C content and excluded homopolymers, such that inclusion of homology arms (24 nt each) resulted in a uniform library length of 300 nt. Final designs are included in Supplementary Table 2.

Design of v2 screen Motif variants were generated from 13 top v1 sequences and tevopreQ1 as follows. On the basis of the expected secondary structure (for example, dot-bracket annotation included in the PseudoBase ref. 52), unpaired nucleotides were iteratively trimmed from both ends to generate shortened sequences (n = 61) with minimally disrupted secondary structures. Next, from each maximally trimmed sequence or tevopreQ1 as the starting point, targeted mutagenesis was performed to maintain secondary structure as follows: (1) double mutations in paired regions (n = 562); (2) double deletions in paired regions (n = 99); (3) double insertions in paired regions (n = 792); (4) single deletions in unpaired regions (n = 85); (5) single substitutions in unpaired regions (n = 366); and (6) double deletions in unpaired regions (n = 54). Pairing interactions in generated sequences included canonical Watson–Crick and the G•U wobble base pair. Along with 11 negative controls (dead or random variants) and 14 positive controls (unmodified v1 sequences), the final list of 2,044 motif variants was paired with five top pegRNAs from the v1 screen (targeting EXM1, PAH, ADA, SCN1A and FBN1) to generate 10,220 assembled epegRNAs. Randomized, GC-balanced linkers were installed between the epegRNA and reverse-complemented synthetic target site (45 nt) to result in a uniform length of 246 nt, after which a 12-nt barcode was added. The assembled insert was flanked by 21-nt homology arms for Gibson assembly. Final designs are listed in Supplementary Table 3.

Design of v3 screen Top variants from the v2 dataset from motif families for Ec (n = 3), FMDVA-2 (n = 11), FMDVO-3 (n = 3), FMDVO-4 (n = 3), HAV1 (n = 8), HPeV1 (n = 15), PhyMV (n = 3), SBRMV1 (n = 16), tevopreQ1 (n = 20), TMEV (n = 3) and WCMV (n = 3) were included as positive controls (n = 88). Within each family, we generated all possible pairwise combinations of mutations present in the selected variants (n = 314 total across all families). We also generated combinations from three of the top variants for FMDVA-2 (n = 13), HAV (n = 3), HPeV1 (n = 4), SBRMV1 (n = 9) and tevopreQ1 (n = 16). Including dead and random negative controls (n = 9), the final list of motifs (n = 453) was paired with 13 prime edits from previous screens or reports81 (to generate 5,889 epegRNAs. Each epegRNA was assigned a unique 20-nt barcode, which was split into 10-nt halves that flanked a 46-nt reverse-complemented synthetic target site. Balancing linkers were introduced between the epegRNA and 66-nt barcode-flanked synthetic target site to have uniform insert length of 258 nt, such that 21-nt cloning homology arms brought the full library length to 300 nt. Sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

From Library ClinVar33, we randomly selected n = 976 edits after applying these filters: (1) exclusion of oligo-U tracts of length ≥ 4 nt; (2) maximum RTT length of 28 nt; (3) maximum edit length of 1 nt (for insertions and deletions); and (4) minimum 5% reported published editing efficiency. As before, we combinatorially generated epegRNAs (n = 19,000) incorporating these edits and motifs and appended a variable-length GC-balanced linker and a reverse0complemented target site (49 nt) flanked by two halves of a unique 16-nt barcode. Flanking 23-nt homology arms resulted in a uniform library of 300 nt. Full sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

Design of v5 screen We took 60 pegRNA sequences from the v4 library and chose six top-performing motifs (eHAV, tevo2.0, HAV, eSBRMV1-A, eFMDVA-2.2 and eFMDVO-4) and n = 4 controls (tevopreQ1, dead tevopreQ1, scrambled tevopreQ1 and no motif). For each pegRNA–motif pair, the tetraloop of the guide scaffold was barcoded with ten redundant but unique 10-bp sequences, yielding a total of 6,000 barcoded pegRNAs. The 10-bp sequences, indicated in Supplementary Table 6, were inserted in between ‘GTTTAAGAGCTATGCTGGA’ and ‘AACAGCATAGCAAGTT- TAAATAAGGCTAGTCCGTTATCAACTTGAAAAAGTGGCACCGAGTCG- GTGC’ sequences in the guide scaffold. We transduced HEK293T cells with a lentiviral pool encoding the v5 library, transfected the cells with either PEmax or PE7 and harvested both genomic DNA (gDNA) and small RNAs. We reverse-transcribed the RNA using a scaffold-specific primer (oSEP0952) and amplified and sequenced the scaffold barcode region to quantify pegRNA representation at the RNA level relative to the corresponding DNA level. For each pegRNA–motif pair, we averaged measurements across the ten barcodes to obtain a normalized estimate of pegRNA abundance. The library was filtered based on having >10 depth-normalized sequencing reads across all DNA and RNA samples analyzed, resulting in 3,860 barcodes being used to evaluate pegRNA abundance. Full sequences are listed in Supplementary Table 6.

General library cloning protocol All high-throughput screening libraries were ordered as single-stranded oligo pools from Twist Biosciences and amplified to prepare a double-stranded library using primers oHS0081 and oHS0082 (Supplementary Table 1) according to recommended protocols using Q5 Hot Start high-fidelity 2× master mix (New England BioLabs, M0494) under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 11–13 cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 68 °C for 30 s and 72 °C for 20 s. Amplified inserts were purified on MinElute PCR purification kit (Qiagen 28004). Isothermal assembly was performed with NEBuilder HiFi DNA assembly master mix (New England BioLabs, E2621) using amplified double-stranded inserts (12 ng) and DpnI-treated (New England BioLabs, R0176) PCR-amplified lentiviral backbone (50 ng; tenfold molar excess) with incubation at 50 °C for 1 h. Assemblies were purified using QIAquick PCR purification kit (Qiagen, 28104) into a minimum volume of double-distilled H2O, electroporated into NEB 10-beta Electrocompetent Escherichia coli (New England Bio- Labs, C3020) according to manufacturer’s instructions and grown on carbenicillin-supplemented (50 µg ml−1) Luria–Bertani agar plates at 1,000× coverage, based on serial dilution plating. After 12–16 h, transfer plasmids were isolated from scraped colonies with the Qiagen Plasmid Plus maxi kit (12963).

Lentivirus packaging and transduction in cell culture For production of lentivirus for self-targeting epegRNA constructs, HEK293T cells were seeded in six-well plates (Corning, 0720083) at a density of 9 × 105 cells per well. At 16 h after seeding, cells were transfected with Lipofectamine 2000 (12 µl; Invitrogen, 11668019) following

the manufacturer’s protocol to deliver transfer plasmid (1,333 ng), pCMV-dR8.2 dvpr (1,000 ng; Addgene, 8455) and pMD2.G (667 ng; Addgene, 12259) in Opti-MEM I reduced-serum medium (250 µl; Gibco, 31985070). The medium was changed 12–18 h after transfection and viral supernatant was collected at 48 h after transfection, centrifuged at 500g for 5 min to remove debris and filtered through 0.45-µm polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) filter (MilliporeSigma, SLHVM33RS) and directly used without further concentration. For PE-PRISM library pools, lentivirus packaging was scaled up 6× in 10-cm dishes for virus production to ensure sufficient virus for library coverage. Cells were transduced aiming for an MOI of 0.3 and ≥1,000× coverage of transduced cells. For transduction of HEK293T cells, the cell culture was supplemented with lentivirus-containing supernatant. For transduction of K562, U2OS, HeLa and N2a cells, spinfection was performed in six-well plates (Corning, 0720083) with 2 × 106 cells in medium supplemented with lentivirus-containing supernatant and 10 µg ml−1 polybrene (MilliporeSigma, TR-1003-G) with centrifugation at 900g for 90 min at 33 °C and the cells were transferred to T75 flasks (Corning, 353136) for recovery at 37 °C, 5% CO2 atmosphere. High-throughput sequencing (HTS) of PE-PRISM screens gDNA from each replicate was subjected to a first round of PCR (PCR1) using Q5 Hot Start high-fidelity 2× master mix (New England BioLabs, M0494L) to amplify the integrated lentiviral cassette and append sequencing adaptors. Each 50-μl reaction contained up to 5 μg of gDNA. Primer sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 1. PCR1 products were purified using the QIAquick PCR purification kit (Qiagen, 28104) and 2 μl (corresponding to 5–10 ng) of purified DNA was used as input for a second PCR (PCR2), which incorporated unique sample indices and flow cell adapters. Final PCR products were bead-purified with a 0.7× ratio of solid-phase reversible immobilization beads, assessed for quality using a TapeStation High-Sensitivity D1000 ScreenTape assay (Agilent) and quantified with the Qubit double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) high-sensitivity assay kit (Invitrogen, Q33231). For screens v1–v4, libraries were then sequenced with a custom Read1 primer (oHS0139) on an Illumina MiSeq, Illumina NextSeq or Element Biosciences AVITI platform for 190 cycles for the R1 read, eight cycles for the i7 index read and eight cycles for the i5 index read. For screen v5, DNA libraries were sequenced with a custom Read1 primer (oSEP0488) on an Illumina MiSeq for 26 cycles for the R1 read, eight cycles for the i7 index read, eight cycles for the i5 index read and 80 cycles for the R2 read. RNA libraries for screen v5 were sequenced without custom primers on an Illumina MiSeq for 35 cycles for the R1 read, eight cycles for the i7 index read, eight cycles for the i5 index read and 70 cycles for the R2 read. Reads were demultiplexed with Bases2Fastq (Element Biosciences) or ‘generate FASTQ’ analysis module (Illumina). For further demultiplexing of individual elements, reads were separated into

individual FASTQ files by alignment to a corresponding member of the library using Bowtie2 (ref. 82) and trimming to exclude scaffold bases. Editing outcomes for each library element were analyzed using CRIS- Presso2 (ref. 83), as described below. Raw data for PE-PRISM screens are included in Supplementary Tables 2–6.

HTS for arrayed experiments Target amplicon sequencing was performed as previously described2. Briefly, PCR1 using primers containing Illumina sequencing adaptors and targeting the genomic locus of interest (primer sequences and modifications in Supplementary Table 1) was templated with 1 µl of cell lysate using Phusion U green multiplex PCR master mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, F564L) under the following conditions: 98 °C for 30 s, followed by 30 cycles of (98 °C for 10 s, 58–68 °C (optimized experimentally) for 20 s and 72 °C for 30 s), with a final extension at 72 °C for 1 min. PCR2 to append unique Illumina barcodes was performed with 1 ml of PCR1 as template under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 98 °C for 30 s, followed by seven cycles of 98 °C for 10 s, 61 °C for 20 s and 72 °C for 30 s), with a final extension at 72 °C for 1 min. Reads were demultiplexed with Bases2Fastq (Element Biosciences) or ‘generate FASTQ’ analysis module (Illumina).

Analysis of PE outcomes Demultiplexed sequencing reads were aligned to a reference sequence using CRISPResso2 (version 2.2.10)83 in batch analysis mode. For all analyses, the discard_indel_reads parameter was set as ‘TRUE’, the q parameter set as ‘30’ and the expected_hdr_amplicon_seq provided as the amplicon sequence containing the intended editing outcome. The quantification window coordinates (‘-qwc’) were set to minimally encompass the pegRNA nick site, the ngRNA nick site (if applicable), the dead sgRNA putative nick site (if applicable; Fig. 3f and Extended Data Fig. 6f) and the end of the extended 3′ flap generated by reverse transcription. The frequency of PE without indels was calculated as (nondiscarded reads aligning to HDR amplicon)/(total reads aligning to all amplicons) and is referred to as ‘editing’ throughout. The frequency of indels was calculated as (total discarded reads)/(total reads aligning to all amplicons). For analysis of pooled PE-PRISM screens to identify top elements, raw data were filtered to exclude library elements that had dropped out (< 50 reads) and elements that showed undetectable editing (< 5 reads). For each unique combination of motif, target protospacer and prime editor, we computed a z score to normalize editing outcomes and account for differences in absolute editing percentage across these variables. Average z scores for each motif were calculated across occurrences throughout the library dataset and biological replicates.

LNP formulation and characterization LNPs were prepared using a microfluidic mixing device84. The ethanol phase was generated by dissolving OF-02 ionizable lipid (Cayman Chemicals, 37652), 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine (DOPE, Avanti Research, 850725), cholesterol (Sigma-Aldrich, C8667) and 1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-[methoxy (polyethylene glycol)-2000] ammonium salt (C14-PEG2000, Avanti Research, 880150) at a molar ratio of 35:16:46.5:2.5 (OF-02:DOPE: Chol:C14-PEG2000). sgRNA with the identical protospacer sequence as the programmed prime edit66. Use of an sgRNA surrogate with the same protospacer for PE was previously reported to nominate largely overlapping sets of genomic loci using CIRCLE-seq16. The 14 sites selected for targeted amplicon sequencing were filtered on the basis of (1) sites with up to 1-nt mismatch in the PAM-proximal region of the nominated protospacer, and (2) sites with the highest CIRLCE-seq read count. Afterwards, ~4.5 ml of the 40–60% interface was extracted using a 16-gauge needle, filtered through a 0.22 μm PES filter, buffer exchanged with 100K MWCO protein concentrators (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 88532) into PBS containing 0.001% Pluronic F-68, and concentrated down to a volume of 200–1000 μl. The concentrated virus was filtered through a 0.22 μm PES filter and stored at 4 °C or −180 °C. To determine AAV titers, 5 μl of each purified virus library were incubated with 100 μl of an endonuclease cocktail consisting of 1000 U ml−1 Turbonuclease (Sigma T4330-50KU) with 1X DNase I reaction buffer (NEB B0303S) in UltraPure DNase/RNase-Free distilled water at 37 °C for one h. Next, the endonuclease solution was inactivated by adding 5 μl of 0.5M EDTA, pH 8.0 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 15575020) and incubated at room temperature for 5 min and then at 70 °C for 10 min. To release the encapsidated AAV genomes, 120 μl of a Proteinase K cocktail consisting of 1M NaCl, 1% N-lauroylsarcosine, 100 μg ml−1 Proteinase K (Qiagen, 19131) in UltraPure DNase/RNase-Free distilled water was added to the mixture and incubated at 56 °C for 2 to 16 h. The Proteinase K-treated samples were then heat-inactivated at 95 °C for 10 min. The released AAV genomes were serial diluted between 460–4,600,000X in dilution buffer consisting of 10X PCR Buffer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, N8080129), 2 μg ml−1 sheared salmon sperm DNA (Thermo Fisher Scientific, AM9680), and 0.05% Pluronic F68 (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 24040032) in UltraPure Water (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Two μl of the diluted samples were used as input in a ddPCR supermix (Bio-Rad, 1863023). Primers and probes, targeting the ITR region, were used for titration, at a final concentration of 900 nM and 250 nM, respectivel (ITR2_Forward: 5’-GGAACCCCTAGTGATGGAGTT; ITR2_Reverse: 5’ is available under a CC-BY-NC-ND 4.0 International license. ITR2_Probe: 5’-CACTCCCTCTCTGCGCGCTCG (FAM/Iowa Black FQ Zen). Droplets were generated using a QX100 Droplet Generator following the manufacturer’s protocol. The droplets were transferred to thermocycler and cycled according to the manufacturer’s protocol with an annealing/ extension of 58 °C for one min. Finally, droplets were read on a QX100 Droplet Digital System to determine titers.

AAV and eVLP administration to mice and tissue processing Microinjection pipettes were generated from PCR micropipettes (Drummond Scientific, 5-000-1001-X10) using a Sutter P1000 puller to obtain a tip diameter of approximately 100 μm. For eVLP treatments, the injection mixture contained 4.6 × 1010 PE-eVLP particles, diluted in 0.9% NaCl (Covetrus, 061758) to a final volume of 4 μl with the addition of 0.3 μl of concentrated eGFP:KASH lentivirus and 0.1 μl of Fast Green. A total of 4 μl of the prepared solution was loaded into the micropipette syringe. For AAV treatments, the injection mixture contained 5 × 1010 of each of N- and C-terminal prime editor AAV9 viruses and 1 × 1010 eGFP:KASH AAV9 virus diluted in 0.9% NaCl (Covetrus, 061758) to a final

volume of 4 μl with the addition of 0.1 μl Fast Green. Neonatal mice were anesthetized on ice and 2 μl of injection mixture was administered into each ventricle. Successful delivery was confirmed by visualization of Fast Green dispersion using head transillumination. Mice were killed by CO2 asphyxiation 3 weeks after eVLP injection and tissues were immediately isolated without perfusion. Samples were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen. Nuclei were extracted using the Miltenyi Biotec nucleus extraction buffer (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-128-024) in combination with the gentleMACS Octo dissociator with heaters (Miltenyi Biotec), as described previously15. All procedures were performed at 4 °C. Dissected brain tissue was resuspended in 2 ml of of complete nucleus extraction buffer (nucleus extraction buffer supplemented with murine RNase inhibitor (New England BioLabs, M0314S) at a final concentration of 0.2 U per μl), transferred into gentleMACS C tubes (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-093-237) and homogenized using the manufacturer’s default program ‘4C_nuclei_1.’ The resulting homogenate was passed through a 100-μm MACS Smart- Strainer into a 15-ml tube, after which 2 ml of additional complete extraction buffer was added. Then, 4 ml of filtrate was centrifuged at 500g for 5 min at 4 °C and the supernatant was discarded. The pellet was resuspended in 4 ml of ice-cold nucleus suspension buffer (PBS containing 100 μg μl−1 albumin (New England BioLabs, B9200S), 3.33 μM Vybrant DyeCycle ruby stain (Thermo Fisher, V10309) and 0.2 U per μl Murine RNase Inhibitor (New England BioLabs, M0314S)) and centrifuged again under the same conditions. The supernatant was removed and the pellet was resuspended in 1 ml of nucleus suspension buffer before being passed through a 35-μm cell strainer (Corning, 352235). Nuclei were then flow-sorted on a Sony MA900 cell sorter (Sony Biotechnology) at the Broad Institute flow cytometry core. Gating was performed using forward and side scatter to identify nuclei, followed by singlet discrimination through DyeCycle ruby intensity. Sorting was subsequently carried out based on GFP fluorescence to isolate bulk and GFP-positive nuclei. Sorted nuclei were collected into RLT Plus buffer (Qiagen, AllPrep DNA/RNA mini kit) and DNA was purified following the manufacturer’s instructions as input for HTS library preparation, as described above.

Computational analysis and RNA structural modeling Computational modeling analysis was performed on (1) full-length epegRNA and (2) 3′ extension in isolation (comprising the RTT, PBS and motif) to simulate a Cas9-bound state. Secondary-structure ensemble properties and minimum free energy (MFE) configurations were calculated using the ViennaRNA package (version 2.7.2). For each sequence, MFE values and base-pairing probability matrices were generated using the ‘fold_compound’ module. The RNAstructure toolkit (version 6.5) was used to characterize the structural ensemble, including calculation of per-nucleotide Shannon entropy and the prediction of pseudoknotted structures using the ‘ProbKnot’ module. For downstream correlation analyses, PBS accessibility was quantified as the average base-pairing probability (pairingprobPBS) for all nucleotides within the PBS region, calculated by summing the rows of the base-pairing probability matrix. Length-normalized free energy (∆Gavg) was calculated by dividing MFE by total sequence length. These values are listed in Supplementary Table 5. For the best-berforming and worst-performing motifs for each edit in the v4 dataset, the performance advantage (z score) was compared against the corresponding differences in structural features (∆pairingprobPBS and ∆∆Gavg).

Quantification and statistical analysis The number of independent biological replicates and/or technical replicates is described in the figure legends or the protocol for each experiment. Data are presented as the mean ± s.d. or as indicated in the corresponding figure legends. Statistical analyses were performed in GraphPad Prism (version 10.5.0) for MacOS. # Article Engineering a genomically recoded organism with one stop codon

Michael W. Grome1,2, Michael T. A. Nguyen1,2,6, Daniel W. Moonan2,3,6, Kyle Mohler2,4,6, Kebron Gurara1,2,6, Shenqi Wang1,2, Colin Hemez1,2,5, Benjamin J. Stenton1,2, Yunteng Cao1,2, Felix Radford1,2, Maya Kornaj1,2,4, Jaymin Patel1,2, Maisha Prome1,2, Svetlana Rogulina2,4, David Sozanski1,2, Jesse Tordoff1,2, Jesse Rinehart2,4 ✉ & Farren J. Isaacs1,2,5 ✉

The genetic code is conserved across all domains of life, yet exceptions have revealed variations in codon assignments and associated translation factors1–3. Inspired by this natural malleability, synthetic approaches have demonstrated whole-genome replacement of synonymous codons to construct genomically recoded organisms (GROs)4,5 with alternative genetic codes. However, no efforts have fully leveraged translation factor plasticity and codon degeneracy to compress translation function to a single codon and assess the possibility of a non-degenerate code. Here we describe construction and characterization of Ochre, a GRO that fully compresses a translational function into a single codon. We replaced 1,195 TGA stop codons with the synonymous TAA in ∆TAG Escherichia coli C321.∆A4. We then engineered release factor 2 (RF2) and tRNATrp to mitigate native UGA recognition, translationally isolating four codons for non-degenerate functions. Ochre thus utilizes UAA as the sole stop codon, with UGG encoding tryptophan and UAG and UGA reassigned for multi-site incorporation of two distinct non-standard amino acids into single proteins with more than 99% accuracy. Ochre fully compresses degenerate stop codons into a single codon and represents an important step toward a 64-codon non-degenerate code that will enable precise production of multi-functional synthetic proteins with unnatural encoded chemistries and broad utility in biotechnology and biotherapeutics.

The standard genetic code contains 64 codons that degenerately encode 20 natural amino acids and translation termination. Organismal variations in codon recognition and inclusion of natural non-standard amino acids (nsAAs) have given rise to alternative genetic codes1–3. Cognate and near-cognate codon recognition by tRNAs can vary widely across domains and between species as tRNAs are gained, lost, mutated or reassigned to recognize different codons—for example, via variations in anticodon wobble and base modifications (such as inosine)1. Deviations in code may render codons unassigned6, encoding alternative canonical amino acids2,3 or nsAAs7,8, or serving as noncanonical stop codons (such as UUA and UCA)7. Alternative codon configurations and codon redundancy highlight the plasticity of the genetic code, motivating genome-scale efforts to construct GROs—organisms constructed with alternative genetic codes whereby redundant codons are reassigned to new functions. GROs possess several advantageous phenotypes, including for enhanced phage resistance8–10, biocontainment strategies11,12 and efficient site-specific incorporation of nsAAs to imbue novel protein properties13,14. The first constructed GRO was an E. coli in which all instances of TAG stop codons were replaced with synonymous TAA codons, followed by deletion of release factor 1 (RF1)4,15. The resulting strain, C321.ΔA, released TAG as an unassigned codon amenable for reassignment.

Recent efforts have commenced to reassign sense codons in E. coli5,16 and other organisms17–19. Whole-genome recoding inspires unresolved questions regarding the malleability of the genetic code and whether a minimal non-degenerate genome is feasible. By assigning unused codons to new functions, such genomes could expand in vivo protein design with unnatural biochemistries, conferring valuable properties for biomaterials and drugs (for example, immunity to proteases). Achieving such goals requires engineering essential translation factors (tRNAs and release factors) for defined single-codon specificities (codon exclusivity), decoupling codons from translational crosstalk (for example, wobble effect or near-cognate suppression) and eliminating functional redundancy among synonymous codons. Single-codon specificities found in nature demonstrate the feasibility of engineering exclusivity—for example, AUG specificity for tRNAMet enabled by discriminatory post-transcriptional modifications of AUG-specific tRNAMet(CAU) and AUA-specific tRNAIle(CAU)20. Eliminating similar modifications has mitigated anticodon wobble in native tRNAs, rendering them codon exclusive21,22. Engineering essential translation factors presents unique challenges related to their cryptic alternative functions that could be revealed by wide-scale genomic recoding efforts.

Here we describe Ochre, a GRO that fully compresses a redundant codon functionality into a single codon, liberating two essential stop codons for reassignment. Specifically, synonymous replacement of 1,195 instances of the stop codon TGA alongside ∆TAG4, combined with engineering of essential translation factors (RF2 and tRNATrp) to attenuate native UGA recognition, enabled multi-site incorporation of two distinct nsAAs at UAG and UGA with greater than 99% accuracy within single proteins. Although past recoding efforts have repurposed stop and sense codons via deletion of associated translation machineries (RF14 and tRNAs5, respectively), a genome reduced to a

single non-degenerate stop codon had not been achieved owing to challenges in engineering translation factors to precisely tune codon specificities. Our efforts disentangled translational crosstalk within the stop codon block, rendering four codons non-degenerate, with each serving a unique function: UAA as the sole stop codon, UGG encoding Trp and UGA and UAG liberated to encode two unique nsAAs (Fig. 1a). Distinct from prior efforts4,5, we demonstrate the importance of compressing redundant codons and disentangling translational crosstalk to fully liberate codons for precise nsAA reassignments, establishing a benchmark for future recoding. ## Constructing a ΔTAG/ΔTGA recoded strain

The stop codon block consists of four translationally linked codons: TAG, TGA, TAA and TGG. In C321.∆A4, TAG is freed as an open coding channel, leaving TAA (stop), TGG (Trp) and TGA (stop and near-cognate Trp). With only 71 essential genes among 1,216 total open reading frames (ORFs) containing TGA in the MG1655 genome (Extended Data Table 1), TGA is the second rarest codon. This scarcity and translational redundancy makes TGA an attractive target alongside TAG. Additionally, dual orthogonal translation systems (OTSs) expressing orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases (o-aaRSs) and tRNAs (o-tRNAs) targeting UAG and UGA have been deployed in unrecoded E. coli to incorporate two distinct nsAAs24, but their efficacy was limited by competition with native translation factors. There are four primary open questions for our recoding effort: (1) whether TGA codons are essential; (2) whether redundant codon functions can be compressed into one codon; (3) whether release factors can attain single-codon specificity; and (4) whether codon suppression can be mitigated without deletion of translation factors. Release factors7,25 and tRNAs26,27 with altered specificities suggest it is feasible to engineer attenuated UGA recognition, mitigating translation factor competition to free TGA alongside TAG for reassignment. Addressing these questions would enable construction of a strain lacking both TAG and TGA codons that, when complemented by a noncompetitive mutant release factor and tRNATrp, could be reassigned as sense codons. Although previous recoding efforts enabled nsAA incorporation at two open serine codons9, unresolved translational crosstalk (for example, o-tRNA wobble28) is likely to result in misincorporations. We hypothesize that resolving crosstalk at UGA within a ∆TGA recoded strain will enable precise, site-specific dual incorporation of nsAAs at both UAG and UGA and establish functional codon exclusivity (non-degeneracy) in the stop codon block. To construct a ΔTAG, ΔTGA recoded strain (rEcΔ2.ΔA), we used the ΔTAG progenitor C321.ΔA4, which we refer to as rEcΔ1.ΔA. All TGA codons, with few exceptions, occur at the end of a gene to terminate translation. Out of the 1,216 annotated ORFs that contain TGA, 1,171 are annotated genes and 45 are listed as pseudogenes. To reduce recoding efforts, 76 non-essential genes and 3 pseudogenes containing TGA were removed with 16 targeted genomic deletions29 (Fig. 1b). The remaining 1,134 terminal TGA codons (1,092 genes and 42 pseudogenes) were targeted for conversion to TAA via multiplex automated genomic engineering (MAGE)30 (Supplementary Table 1). Three formate dehydrogenase genes (fdhF, fdoG and fdnG) containing internal TGA codons were not targeted for recoding owing to their role in encoding selenocysteine31. Four distinct oligonucleotide designs were used to convert codons. One strategy introduced single-nucleotide substitutions to 833 non-overlapping ORFs and 3 refactoring strategies targeted 380 overlapping ORFs in which such substitutions might affect neighbouring gene expression (Fig. 1c and Supplementary Methods). These latter strategies resulted in changes to more than 300 overlapping coding sequences (Supplementary Table 2) and few predicted disruptions to translation initiation rates (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Table 3). Construction of ΔTGA rEcΔ2.ΔA constituted two major phases (Fig. 1e), each utilizing iterative cycles of MAGE30 concurrently targeting distinct genomic subdomains within clonal progenitor strains, followed by conjugative assembly genome engineering (CAGE)15 to hierarchically assemble recoded subdomains into a final strain. TGA-to-TAA conversions were confirmed via whole-genome sequencing (WGS) after each assembly. In phase 1, rEcΔ2E.ΔA was constructed from rEcΔ1.ΔA by

converting 71 essential genes terminating with TGA split between 2 distinct genomic subdomains (A′ and B′) among two clones (Supplementary Table 4). An additional 44 proximal genes terminating with TGA were converted and 3 genes terminating with TGA were replaced with selectable markers. Recoded subdomains A′ and B′ were assembled via CAGE into rEcΔ2E.ΔA (Supplementary Table 5). Phase 2 constructed the final ΔTGA recoded rEcΔ2.ΔA. Another 1,012 ORFs terminating with TGA (980 genes and 35 pseudogenes) were converted via MAGE (Supplementary Table 1 and 6) and 229 non-essential ORFs (72 genes terminating with TGA and 3 pseudogenes terminating with TGA)29 were deleted via marker placements (Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 7). TGA sites were divided among eight rEcΔ2E.ΔA clones and targeted concurrently across distinct genomic subdomains (A–H) split among clones (Fig. 1b and Supplementary Table 8). Preserving chemotaxis and motility, non-essential genomic regions were identified29 and those with a high density of genes terminating with TGA were deleted, yielding 16 genomic deletions. Unwanted markers were deleted via tolC displacements15. The non-essential glycerate kinase I gene garK was recalcitrant to conversion and was inactivated by a frameshift nonsense mutation (Supplementary Table 9). Recoded subdomains were hierarchically assembled via CAGE into the final rEcΔ2.ΔA (Extended Data Fig. 2 and Supplementary Table 10). Out of 1,216 predicted TGA codons in E. coli, 1,195 were abolished, leaving 10 predicted pseudogenes, 8 insertion sequences and 3 internal selenocysteine codons unrecoded (Extended Data Table 1). WGS data and breseq analysis32 were used to assess background mutations33. More than 700 unintended background mutations accumulated in our final recoded strain (Supplementary Tables 11–13), although this was likely to be an overestimate (Supplementary Methods). To mitigate detrimental phenotypes arising during construction, cell colonies were routinely measured for maximum OD600 (MaxOD) and doubling time in lysogeny broth (LB) and minimal (M9) media. The fastest growing strains with highest MaxOD were selected to progress for further recoding. When auxotrophies arose, conjugal backcrossing to parental strains (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Fig. 2) and targeted reversions of implicated mutations (Supplementary Methods and Supplementary Tables 14a and 15) were used to restore prototrophy.

## Engineering mutant RF2

Engineering UAA-specific translation termination is a first step in decoupling UGA translational crosstalk and liberating UAG and UGA for efficient reassignment. RF1, encoded by prfA, terminates translation at UAG and UAA, whereas RF2, encoded by prfB, terminates translation at UGA and UAA. RF1 was deleted within ancestral rEcΔ1.∆A4, confirming that RF1 is non-essential without TAG codons and that RF2 can serve as the sole release factor. After ∆TGA recoding, we tested whether RF1 could independently support translation termination. Unlike RF1, RF2 serves additional roles beyond termination, including post-peptidyl transfer quality control with release factor 3 (RF3)34 and ArfA-cooperative ribosomal rescue from ‘non-stop’ mRNAs35. Our inability to delete RF2 in the presence of RF1 suggests that RF1 cannot functionally compensate for loss of RF2. The capacity of RF2 to act as a sole release factor made it our target for engineering specificity for UAA. Thus, we sought to identify mutations that attenuate RF2-mediated termination at UGA while retaining essential functions. Using MAGE, five primary mutations were introduced to the prfB gene: (1) T246A, to restore wild-type release factor methylation36,37; (2) terminal TGA-to-TAA conversion; (3) internal TGA-to-TAA for autoregulatory maintenance38,39; (4) S205P for UAA-specific termination activity40; and (5) E170K charge flip41,42 to enable strain viability (Fig. 2a,b and Supplementary Table 14b). Two in vivo assays measured the effect of these mutations on the ability of RF2 to: (1) outcompete cognate/ near-cognate suppression in fluorescent reporter translation; and (2) inhibit phage infection. Although the CUU-UGA sequence is highly conserved in prfB mRNA, exceptions such as Chlorobium tepidum instead have CUU-UAA38, suggesting permissibility. In prokaryotic translation, release factor codon specificity is predominantly conferred by helix α5, specific to U at position 1 of the stop codon, and a 10 or more amino acid codon recognition loop whose structure and sequence discriminates between the second

and third codon bases43–45. Alternative release factor codon specificity is well precedented in prokaryotic systems. Single point mutations in RF2 alter codon specificity (for example, E167K or F207T), expanding recognition to all three stop codons, creating ‘omnipotent’ release factors41. In addition, some mitochondrial release factors terminate at canonical sense codons (for example, AGA or AGG)7. Various works have interrogated codon specificity via tripeptide ‘anticodon’ motifs located within recognition loops: PXT in RF1 (where X is A or V) or SPF in RF243,46,47. Crystallography implicates hydrogen bonding by the threonine in PXT and the serine in SPF in discrimination at the second base of the codon44, although molecular dynamics simulations dispute this45. We hypothesized that one characterized E. coli RF2 mutation (S205P) in the tripeptide SPF might endow UAA specificity within rEcΔ2.∆A46. Structural prediction by AlphaFold48 (Fig. 2b) suggests that wild-type S205 presents up to 4 hydrogen bonds within the codon recognition loop of RF2, whereas P205 presents 1, probably altering recognition loop stability. Previous characterizations of S205P evaluated release factor codon recognition in vivo and in vitro41,46. ## Characterizing mutant RF2 termination

To assess whether RF2.B3 abolishes recognition of UGA, we conducted an in vivo assay measuring release activity of RF2 variants at all three

stop codons. Using validated methods50, this assay evaluates the ability of a release factor to terminate translation of an mCherry gene ending in a target codon upstream of a YFP gene (Fig. 2c, Extended Data Fig. 5b–d and Supplementary Table 18). If no termination occurs at the target codon, translation reads through mCherry to YFP, expressing both proteins. If termination occurs, only mCherry is expressed, yielding low YFP fluorescence. Figure 2d–f presents fluorescence of mCherry and YFP expression as a function of termination at a target codon, normalized to fluorescent expression from GCG (positive control). The results revealed low YFP expression at all stop codons, regardless of release factor status (Fig. 2e). Previous work showed that rEcΔ1.ΔA genes terminating with TAG are degraded via transfer messenger RNA (tmRNA) tagging, reducing UAG codon readthrough and GFP expression51. This is consistent with low expression levels observed for the mCherry gene terminating with UAG and downstream YFP. For more robust readouts, we used modified UAG- and UGA-suppressor serine tRNAs (supD)52 that precisely base pair with their respective codons to examine direct codon competition with release factor variants, effective for assessing codon reassignment (Fig. 2f). Results with mutant rEc∆2.∆A. B3 suggest termination at UAA, approximately 42-fold enhanced readthrough at UAG and 45-fold enhanced readthrough at UGA relative to no suppressors, leading to 11-fold and 8-fold increases in UGA YFP fluorescence compared with wild-type RF2 strains rEc∆1.∆A.B0 and rEc∆2.∆A.B1, respectively. These results demonstrate that UGA recognition by RF2.B3 is significantly attenuated compared with RF2. B0, as RF2.B3 is outcompeted by UGA-specific suppressor tRNAs. To assess whether S205P (not E170K) causes attenuation, we reverted RF2.B3 P205 back to serine, generating variant RF2.B4. We repeated the in vivo mCherry–YFP readthrough assays without suppressors to assess rEc∆2.A.B2 (RF2(S205P)/RF1+) alongside isogenic rEc∆2.∆A.B4 (RF2(E170K)/∆RF1) and two wild-type RF2/∆RF1 controls: rEc∆2.∆A. B0 and rEc∆1.∆A.B0 (Extended Data Fig. 5e). The high mCherry and low YFP fluorescence for UAG from rEc∆2.A.B2 is indicative of RF1 terminating at UAG. For UGA, results reveal low YFP fluorescence from both RF2.B0 and RF2.B4 variants, suggesting little effect from E170K and D26N on UGA termination. However, S205P in the absence of E170K (rEc∆2.A.B2) results in high YFP fluorescence, suggesting significant UGA readthrough from native suppression and possibly abolition of RF2 termination. This result stands in stark contrast to RF2. B3 (S205P with E170K) without supD suppressors (Fig. 2e), revealing S205P to be uniquely responsible for attenuation of UGA termination. These data suggest that E170K restores S205P termination at UAA sufficient for cell viability and partially restores termination at UGA, although significantly attenuated, to enable robust supD suppression (Fig. 2f). The effects of individual RF2 mutations on translation are further evidenced by phage assays assessing genetic orthogonality8–10 (Supplementary Discussion 2). We challenged strains with infection from two bacteriophages: Lambda (λ) (containing TAG, TGA and TAA) and Mu (µ) (containing TGA and TAA only) (Fig. 3 and Extended Data Fig. 6). Whereas all strains lacking RF1 retained resistance to λ, as previously described51 (Fig. 3a), only rEc∆2.A.B2 (RF2(S205P)/RF1+) displayed resistance to µ (Fig. 3b). These results suggest that: (1) UGA termination may be abolished in rEc∆2.A.B2 and thus is not necessary for ∆TGA strain viability; and (2) that E170K in rEc∆2.A.B3 restores partial UGA termination function in alignment with readthrough data.

evaluate OTS activity and native tRNATrp suppression at UGA (Fig. 4b). We observed a significant reduction in YFP/mCherry expression in rEc∆2.∆A.B3.tW* compared with rEc∆2.∆A.B3 (wild-type tRNATrp), suggesting a reduction of native tRNATrp suppression (Fig. 4c). To confirm decreased Trp suppression in rEc∆2.∆A.B3.tW*, we used mass spectrometry reporter for exact amino acid decoding (MS-READ) to assay amino acid incorporation at UGA in wild-type and A37G tRNATrp strains containing Mj-TyrOTS13,55. Mass spectrometry analysis confirmed Mj-TyrOTS-mediated Tyr incorporation at UGA codons, and unexpectedly, a small amount (less than 1%) of Cys incorporation, possibly due to a parallel third base wobble to Sc-tRNACys22. Whereas Trp was the most abundant amino acid at UGA in rEc∆2.∆A.B3 cells with wild-type tRNATrp, it was completely absent in rEc∆2.∆A.B3.tW* (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Table 19). These results confirm that a single base substitution in Ec-tRNATrp preserves native Trp decoding while eliminating UGA suppression, removing the wobble effect and establishing an open UGA codon for reassignment. With the combination of RF1 deletion and attenuated UGA recognition of RF2.B3 and tW*, four codons that naturally display translational crosstalk (UAG-open, UGA-open, UAA-stop and UGG-Trp) can be rendered translationally isolated and functionally exclusive (Fig. 1a).
